input_signals.name: Cheap And Internally Funded Investment
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 1), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheap firms that fund whatever they invest out of internal resources, rather than by issuing debt or equity, are disciplined allocators; expensive firms tapping external capital markets to finance expansion are the classic overvalued-equity-issuance combination.
input_signals.reasoning: External finance raised (change in long-term debt plus stock issuance, scaled by assets) is the funding-side counterpart of aggressive investment and is precisely when managers exploit high valuations, so pairing it with earnings yield captures the mispricing channel directly. COALESCE treats unreported issuance proceeds as zero, which is the economically correct convention for firms with no equity issuance in the year. The mechanism differs from asset-growth screens because it identifies who paid for the growth.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( ib, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( ratio( add( delta( dltt, 1 ), coalesce( sstk, 0 ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Expensive Empire Builder Short
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), RANK(ADD(GROWTH(at, 1), RATIO(COALESCE(aqc, 0), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The most reliable half of the interaction is the short side: firms with rich market-to-book multiples that simultaneously expand organically and through acquisitions systematically disappoint as overvalued growth narratives.
input_signals.reasoning: Multiplying the market-to-book rank by the rank of total expansion intensity (asset growth plus acquisition spending) makes the signal large only when high price expectations and empire-building coincide, isolating the overvaluation-plus-overinvestment corner of the joint distribution. Including aqc separately captures inorganic expansion that asset growth alone can understate for serial acquirers, with unreported acquisitions set to zero. High values should predict low future returns, giving a negative expected slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), rank( add( growth( at, 1 ), ratio( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Maintenance Adjusted Free Cash Flow Yield
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, MA(capx, 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What investors underprice is cash flow that survives the capital spending needed to sustain the business; a high yield on cash flow net of normalized capital expenditure identifies cheap firms whose investment program is modest, while heavy investors have their apparent cheapness eliminated by the deduction.
input_signals.reasoning: Netting three-year average capex out of operating cash flow before scaling by market capitalization embeds investment intensity inside the valuation multiple with market cap—always strictly positive—as the only denominator, which removes the explosive behavior of dividing by a near-zero capex/at. The 3-year moving average treats capex as a normalized maintenance requirement rather than a lumpy annual number, so the signal ranks firms by durable distributable cheapness instead of by inverse capex intensity. It remains a true interaction because the same operating-cash-flow yield maps to very different signal values depending on the firm's investment burden.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( oancf, ma( capx, 3 ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Industry Neutral EBITDA Yield Over Capacity Investment Rate
input_signals.expression: SUB(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, MA(ppegt, 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Within an industry, firms priced cheaply on operating earnings while reinvesting at a low rate relative to their installed capacity base are disciplined operators the market extrapolates too pessimistically; peers with rich multiples and high capacity reinvestment rates are overvalued growth stories that will face overcapacity and falling returns on capital.
input_signals.reasoning: The sign is now stated consistently with the expression: high values mean cheap-and-restrained and predict high returns, low values mean expensive-and-expanding and predict low returns, so the Fama-MacBeth slope should be positive and the long-minus-short FF5 alpha positive. Replacing gross-PPE growth with the capex-to-average-gross-PPE reinvestment rate measures investment intensity relative to installed capacity rather than a one-year balance-sheet change, which is less mechanically related to CMA's asset-growth construction. Industry z-scoring of both legs removes the strong sector clustering in EBITDA multiples and capital intensity so the spread is a firm-level interaction, not a sector bet.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_zscore( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( ratio( capx, ma( ppegt, 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capital Discipline Within Cheap Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The value premium is not uniform: within the cheapest 30% of firms, those reinvesting at a low rate relative to installed net plant are genuinely disciplined and underpriced, while cheap firms plowing cash into their existing capital base are value traps whose price is low for a reason.
input_signals.reasoning: Conditioning on membership in the cheap group and then sorting only on reinvestment intensity makes both tails value-tilted, so the HML exposure of the long and short legs is matched and the spread isolates the value-trap discrimination channel rather than reproducing HML. The capex-to-net-PPE reinvestment rate is investment-exclusive and is a flow measure of capital deployment, which overlaps only partially with CMA's asset-growth factor. Zeros for the non-cheap 70% keep the extreme portfolios entirely inside the value group, which is the intended experiment.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap And Cutting Reinvestment Conjunction
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm signals genuine capital discipline not by a low investment level but by actively reducing its reinvestment rate; when this turn toward restraint occurs in a cheaply priced firm, the market has not yet repriced the coming improvement in free cash flow.
input_signals.reasoning: The minimum of two ranks is an AND gate, so the top of the distribution contains only firms that are simultaneously cheap and cutting reinvestment, a strictly non-linear combination that no weighted sum of HML and CMA can reproduce. Using the one-year change in the capex-to-net-PPE rate rather than its level makes the investment leg a deceleration concept that CMA, a level-of-investment factor, should not absorb — the specific reason gen-0 level-based signals lost their alpha. Both inputs come from universally reported items, so coverage should be comparable to the gen-0 archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( capx, ppent ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap With Rising Labor Productivity
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), GROWTH(RATIO(sale, emp), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Investment discipline shows up in the workforce as well as in plant: firms that raise revenue per employee are extracting more output from existing labor capacity instead of hiring into growth, and when such operating discipline coexists with a high EBITDA yield the market is underpricing an improving, self-funding business.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes the economic channel from capital expenditure to labor input, a dimension of investment that neither CMA nor any capex-based control captures, so its predictive content has a better chance of surviving the five-factor benchmark. Revenue per employee growth is a productivity-of-investment measure rather than a quantity-of-investment measure, which distinguishes it from every gen-0 construction. Employment is broadly reported in Compustat, so coverage should not deteriorate relative to the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), growth( ratio( sale, emp ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Profit Growth Per Unit Of Capital Growth Amplified By Cheapness
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(GROWTH(ebitda, 1), GROWTH(ppent, 1)), RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Investment quality is revealed when operating profit grows faster than the capital base that produced it, and this evidence is most mispriced where the market has assigned the lowest multiple: cheap firms whose profits are outrunning their capital stock are underappreciated disciplined allocators, while cheap firms adding capital without profit are genuine value traps.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing DELTA(ebitda)/MA(capx,3) with the scale-free wedge between EBITDA growth and net-PPE growth removes the near-zero-capex denominator that made the previous version collapse into an inverse-investment-level (CMA) sort, so the signal now measures productivity of capital rather than quantity of capital. Dividing by the cross-sectional rank of market-to-book — a strictly positive, bounded quantity — amplifies the wedge among cheap firms and compresses it toward zero among expensive ones, producing a multiplicative valuation-times-investment-quality interaction instead of the HML-dominated additive rank sum. Both inputs need only one annual lag, so coverage should be at least as good as the gen-0 archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( growth( ebitda, 1 ), growth( ppent, 1 ) ), rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Working Capital Buildup Weighted By Sales Yield
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(GROWTH(RATIO(invt, sale), 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Inventory rising faster than sales is investment in working capital that has not yet been validated by demand, and this overinvestment is most damaging in firms already priced at high sales-to-price multiples, where the market is skeptical about demand in the first place.
input_signals.reasoning: Two things change relative to the gated family: the conditioning is continuous — the cheapness rank is a bounded positive weight that amplifies the discipline signal smoothly instead of switching it off — and the investment concept moves from fixed capital to working capital, which no FF5 factor represents. Comparing this against the hard-gated signals isolates whether the alpha comes from the conditioning shape or from the underlying interaction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sale, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), neg( winsor( zscore( growth( ratio( invt, sale ), 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Investment Instability Within Cheap Half
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(VOL(RATIO(capx, ppent), 3)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital discipline is a process, not a level: among cheap firms, those whose reinvestment rate is stable year to year are running a predictable harvesting strategy, while those whose capital spending swings erratically are making opportunistic, poorly governed bets that the market underestimates the cost of.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the batch's most distinct mechanism because it uses a second moment of investment rather than its level or change, a dimension that CMA cannot span by construction and that the archive has never tested. A three-year volatility window keeps coverage close to the archive's 0.12-0.13 range while still capturing spending erraticism, and the cheap-half gate preserves the leg-matching that has been the only reliable route to positive FF5 alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.5 ), neg( winsor( zscore( vol( ratio( capx, ppent ), 3 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Serial Acquisition Spending Within Cheap Half
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, 0), 3), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Value firms with weak organic prospects that respond by repeatedly buying other companies are diworsifying, and the three-year cumulative cash outlay on acquisitions identifies the serial acquirers among them; cheap firms that abstain are the disciplined allocators.
input_signals.reasoning:
Replacing the change in goodwill with cash acquisition outlays removes the impairment contamination the critic identified — aqc is a cash-flow-statement investing outflow that can only be positive spending, so the long leg no longer buys firms writing down past mistakes — and it is reported consistently across the full sample rather than only post-SFAS-142. Cumulating over three years targets serial acquisitiveness as a management style rather than a single lumpy deal, which is the behavioral trait the hypothesis is about, and zero is the economically correct value for non-acquirers.
REASONING_NOTE: Inorganic expansion remains a distinct channel from the organic capex measures already in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.5 ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), 3 ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Reinvestment Discipline In Both Valuation Tails
input_signals.expression: MUL(ADD(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Reinvestment intensity is informative about returns only where price expectations are extreme — among deep-value firms it separates harvesters from value traps, and among glamour firms it separates asset-light compounders from empire builders — while for middling valuations capital spending carries no mispricing content.
input_signals.reasoning: This doubles the informative mass of the archive's best design from 30% to 60% of the universe, directly fixing the thin-tail and degenerate-breakpoint problem the critic identified, and it does so by adding an economically motivated second gate rather than by nudging a percentile. It is also a diagnostic: if alpha survives or strengthens, the interaction lives in both valuation tails; if it collapses, the mispricing is specific to the value side and future work should stay there.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( add( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), indicator( neg( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), -0.3 ) ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Total Operating Capital Absorption Within Cheap Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(ADD(capx, DELTA(invt, 1)), ADD(ppent, invt))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What drains a cheap firm's distributable cash is the total capital it absorbs, fixed plus working, so the right discipline measure is combined capital absorption per dollar of operating capital already employed; firms with low total absorption are harvesters and those with high absorption are consuming the very cash flow the low multiple is supposed to represent.
input_signals.reasoning:
Instead of blending the ranks of two evaluated signals, this builds a single new accounting quantity — capex plus the change in inventory over plant plus inventory — which is the firm's total incremental claim on operating capital and is not the sum of two previously tested sorts. Because the denominator includes inventory, the measure is meaningful for distribution- and retail-type value firms whose capital is in stock rather than plant, extending the winning mechanism to firms where capx/ppent is uninformative, and no giant tie block enters the construction beyond the intended valuation gate.
REASONING_NOTE: Positive denominator by construction, so no explosive scaling.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( add( capx, delta( invt, 1 ) ), add( ppent, invt ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Congruence With Lagged Capital Deployment
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(LAG(capx, 2), ppent)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Congruence is best judged against the spending that has already had time to show up in operations: a cheap firm that expanded two years ago carries unrecognized overcapacity, while an expensive firm whose earlier expansion is now maturing is delivering on the growth the multiple assumed.
input_signals.reasoning: This combines the archive's two largest alphas — the cheap-gate discipline signal at +4.2% and the two-year-lagged capex overhang signal at +5.1% (t=1.9) — inside the congruence form the sign evidence supports, so it tests whether the timing dimension and the functional form reinforce each other. The lag also mitigates the simultaneity concern that current capex and current price both respond to the same contemporaneous news, which should help the FMB slope that the overhang signal left weak at 1.27.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( zscore( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( lag( capx, 2 ), ppent ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Unvalidated Expansion Within Glamour Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3), WINSOR(ZSCORE(SUB(GROWTH(ppent, 1), GROWTH(ebitda, 1))), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Among the most richly valued firms, the ones whose capital base is growing faster than their operating profits are expanding without validation — the multiple already prices growth that the income statement is not delivering — while expensive firms whose profits are outrunning their capital base are genuinely converting expansion into earnings.
input_signals.reasoning:
This drops the back-fitted claim that heavy investment per se is good among glamour firms and replaces it with a sign that agrees with the investment anomaly: expansion is penalized, but only the portion unmatched by profit growth, which is the economically meaningful part. Both legs of the spread sit inside the expensive tail, so the growth tilt is matched and the spread cannot be a repackaged short-HML position; the discriminator is a capital-versus-profit wedge, not a capex level, so it is also not spanned by CMA.
REASONING_NOTE: The gate selects the cheapest-30%-complement, i.e. book-to-market rank below 0.3.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( neg( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), -0.3 ), winsor( zscore( sub( growth( ppent, 1 ), growth( ebitda, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Soft Asset Bloat Within Cheap Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Not all asset expansion is capacity: for cheap firms the most damaging growth is in non-physical operating assets — receivables, inventory, acquired intangibles — which represents bloat and soft accounting rather than productive capacity, while cheap firms holding these assets flat are running a tight operation.
input_signals.reasoning:
Replacing acquisition outlays with the change in non-cash, non-plant operating assets removes the degeneracy the critic identified — that leg is continuously distributed across essentially all firms instead of being zero for most of them, so the signal can never collapse into plain book-to-market. It also isolates a channel the archive has not tested: physical capacity expansion and soft-asset expansion are economically different, and the value-matched gate keeps both spread legs inside the cheap group so the alpha cannot come from a value tilt.
REASONING_NOTE: Cash is subtracted so that hoarding liquidity is not counted as investment, and net plant is subtracted so the measure is orthogonal to the capex channel already in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( delta( sub( sub( at, che ), ppent ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Persistent Soft Asset Bloat Within Cheap Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 3), LAG(at, 3))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Bloat in non-cash, non-plant operating assets is damaging when it is a persistent multi-year accumulation rather than a single-year fluctuation, because sustained buildup of receivables, inventory, and acquired intangibles reflects a business model that quietly consumes capital while its low multiple suggests otherwise.
input_signals.reasoning: The one-year version of this discriminator is the archive's best joint result (FMB 2.83, alpha +3.7%, t=2.65), and the separate expansion-overhang evidence (alpha +5.1% on two-year-lagged capex) says multi-year measurement of investment carries more return-relevant information than the current year, so the timing axis is the highest-value refinement available. A three-year change also averages out working-capital seasonality and one-off acquisitions, which should raise the FMB t-stat rather than merely the alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( delta( sub( sub( at, che ), ppent ), 3 ), lag( at, 3 ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Industry Neutral Soft Asset Bloat Within Cheap Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Normal rates of working-capital and intangible-asset growth differ sharply across industries — distributors and pharma acquirers naturally carry high soft-asset growth — so bloat that signals mismanagement must be judged relative to industry peers rather than the whole market.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best signal has a raw Sharpe of −0.10 despite a strong FF5 alpha, which is the signature of a spread whose raw return is offset by a persistent sector or factor tilt; industry z-scoring the discriminator is the diagnostic and the likely fix, since it removes the static sector composition while leaving the firm-level bloat information intact. If both the FMB slope and the alpha t-stat improve, future work should be industry-neutral throughout.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), neg( winsor( ind_zscore( ratio( delta( sub( sub( at, che ), ppent ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft Asset Bloat Within Glamour Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expensive firms accumulating non-cash, non-plant operating assets are capitalizing growth into the balance sheet without the cash flow to show for it, and this soft expansion should predict underperformance among glamour names just as unvalidated plant growth does.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the mirror experiment to Signal 2 and completes a clean 2x2 of the archive's two best discriminators against the two valuation tails, which is the cheapest way to learn whether these mispricings are tail-specific or general before committing the remaining generations. The gate keeps both spread legs inside the expensive group, so a negative alpha here cannot be a disguised short-HML position.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( neg( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), -0.3 ), winsor( zscore( ratio( delta( sub( sub( at, che ), ppent ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Working Capital Bloat Excluding Intangibles Within Cheap Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), COALESCE(intan, 0)), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The soft-asset result should be driven by operating bloat that management controls directly — receivables extended to weak customers and inventory built ahead of demand — rather than by purchased intangibles, because working-capital expansion reflects deteriorating business quality while intangible additions reflect discrete acquisition decisions.
input_signals.reasoning: Stripping intangibles out of the winning discriminator is a direct attribution test: if the alpha survives, the mechanism is operating-cycle bloat and future work should refine working capital; if it collapses, the mechanism is acquisitive growth and the design should switch to acquisition measures. It also removes the goodwill-impairment contamination that made earlier intangible-based proposals uninterpretable, since write-downs no longer enter the measure at all.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( delta( sub( sub( sub( at, che ), ppent ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft Asset Bloat Across Both Valuation Tails
input_signals.expression: MUL(ADD(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Soft-asset bloat predicts underperformance with the same sign in both valuation tails — cheap bloaters are value traps and expensive bloaters are capitalizing growth they cannot fund from cash — so conditioning on extreme valuation of either kind, rather than on cheapness alone, should double the informative breadth without sign cancellation.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike the reinvestment-intensity discriminator, whose two-tail extension reversed the alpha to −4.5%, the bloat discriminator has now been shown to have a correctly signed and even stronger FMB slope in the glamour tail (−3.86), so the two tails should reinforce rather than offset and the pooled design is a genuine test of breadth rather than a repeat of a known failure. The result also discriminates the two competing readings of the archive: that valuation gating works because value firms are special, or that it works because mispricing concentrates wherever price expectations are extreme.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( add( indicator( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 0.7 ), indicator( neg( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), -0.3 ) ), neg( winsor( zscore( ratio( delta( sub( sub( at, che ), ppent ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Simultaneous Restraint Conjunction Within Cheap Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), MIN(NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuine capital discipline must hold on both fronts at once: a cheap firm earns the harvester label only if it is simultaneously restrained in plant spending and in soft-asset accumulation, because a firm restrained on just one dimension is typically relocating expansion to the other part of the balance sheet rather than returning cash.
input_signals.reasoning:
The minimum of the two restraint scores implements the conjunction the hypothesis asserts — a firm is scored by its weaker dimension, so extreme restraint in plant cannot offset soft-asset bloat, which is exactly what the additive version wrongly permitted. This makes the signal a genuine non-linear AND gate over two orthogonal balance-sheet channels, and the short tail identifies firms expanding on at least one front, testing the substitution story that neither component alone can address.
REASONING_NOTE: All ranking is done inside the cheap tail's gate, so both spread legs retain matched value exposure.

input_signals.hypothesis: The danger of soft-asset accumulation depends on the equity cushion that must absorb it: for a levered cheap firm, a build equal to a fifth of book equity can wipe out its solvency margin if the receivables prove uncollectible or the inventory must be marked down, whereas the same build against a large unlevered equity base is easily absorbed.

It also gives a testable prediction distinct from the existing family: if the bloat effect is really about the fragility of the equity cushion, the equity-deflated version should dominate the asset-deflated one, and if it is purely about capital absorption the two should perform alike.
